t: Initiates, the syndexioi or “those united by the handshake”, passed through seven grades and met for ritual meals in small underground temples, the mithraea, made to represent the cave where Mithras killed the bull.
Soldiers were strongly represented, with merchants, customs officials, freedmen and slaves, and the cult spread through Rome and Ostia, the Rhine and Danube frontiers, North Africa and Britain.

Its origins are still debated: Franz Cumont saw it as the Roman form of the Persian religion, but since the 1970s scholars have generally rejected his model, many seeing a new creation of the Roman world.
dyk: Votive coins scattered over the floor of the mithraeum at Pons Sarravi (Sarrebourg) in Gallia Belgica run from Gallienus to Theodosius I: when the temple was destroyed, Christians apparently regarded the coins as polluted and left them behind.
ev: Cilician pirates are said to practise “secret rites” of Mithras, though whether this bears on the origins of the mysteries is unclear
Tiridates I of Armenia, crowned by Nero, tells the emperor that he reveres him “as Mithras”
Statius’s Thebaid, one of the earliest literary references, pictures Mithras in a cave; the first mithraea appear
Justin Martyr charges the cult of Mithras with imitating the Christian communion
The Virunum album records a Mithraic festival of commemoration on 26 June
Mithraists face persecution from Christians, and their sanctuaries are destroyed
Votive coins at Sarrebourg end with the reign of Theodosius I, near the end of the cult
At the First International Congress of Mithraic Studies, John R. Hinnells and R. L. Gordon severely criticise Cumont’s theory of Persian origins

f.origin: the Roman Empire, where its earliest temples appear in the last quarter of the 1st century CE, apparently with its centre in Rome; inspired by Iranian worship of Mithra, though how far it continued Persian practice is debated
f.founder: none known: Merkelbach, Clauss and Beck think a founder or founders created the mysteries in Rome, while others see a continuation of Iranian Mithra worship
f.scriptures: none survive: no written narratives or theology, only an oath, a catechism fragment, graffiti and inscriptions, and passing references in Greek and Latin writers; the histories of Mithras by Pallas and Euboulus are lost
f.followers: none: persecuted by Christians in the 4th century, it was suppressed and came to an end between the last decade of that century and the 5th century
